title: Cardiogenic Shock 2026 Update by CSWG
excerpt: A new 2026 report from the Cardiogenic Shock Working Group (CSWG), published in the Journal of Cardiac Failure, proposes an updated staging system designed to make assessment of shock severity simpler, more objective, and applicable across different clinical settings.
body:
Why Was an Update Needed?

The original Society for Cardiovascular Angiography and Interventions (SCAI) staging system, introduced in 2019, established a common language for describing cardiogenic shock severity from stage A (at risk) to stage E (extremis).

In 2022, the CSWG introduced more objective thresholds using several clinical variables, including blood pressure, lactate, pH, alanine aminotransferase (ALT), and the intensity of circulatory support.

However, some limitations remained:

  • Certain clinical presentations were not adequately captured by existing lactate thresholds.

  • Classification relied on multiple variables, increasing complexity.

  • Out-of-hospital cardiac arrest automatically triggered stage E classification, regardless of subsequent hemodynamic recovery.

  • Treatment intensity and its relationship to severity required further clarification.

The 2026 update addresses these limitations using a much larger contemporary dataset.

The Study: Evidence From Nearly 1.5 Million Patients

Investigators analyzed 11,640 patients enrolled in the multicenter CSWG registry between 2021 and 2025, including patients with heart failure-related cardiogenic shock (HF-CS) and myocardial infarction-related cardiogenic shock (MI-CS).

They examined relationships between clinical parameters, treatment intensity, and in-hospital mortality, including serial measurements during the first 72 hours after shock diagnosis.

The revised classification was then evaluated in an independent population of 1,417,637 patients across 161 hospitals in 20 US states.

The aim was not to create a complex mortality prediction score, but to improve the practicality and consistency of bedside shock classification.

What Has Changed in the 2026 Classification?

1. Three clinical parameters replace a more complex assessment

The updated system focuses on:

Systolic blood pressure (SBP)

  • ≥90 mmHg

  • 60 to less than 90 mmHg

  • Less than 60 mmHg

Serum lactate

  • 0–2 mmol/L

  • 2–5 mmol/L

  • 5–10 mmol/L

  • 10 mmol/L

Treatment intensity

The total number of simultaneously administered vasoactive drugs and tMCS devices:

  • Stage C: typically 1–2

  • Stage D: typically 3–4

  • Stage E: ≥5

These treatment-count thresholds are components of the staging system, not standalone definitions. The full stage assignment also depends on blood pressure, lactate, and clinical circumstances.

Mean arterial pressure (MAP), pH, and ALT are no longer required for staging.

Although pH and mean arterial pressure correlated with mortality, SBP and lactate were retained for simplicity and consistency with existing cardiogenic shock trials. ALT showed relatively little association with mortality.

Importantly, adding the vasoactive-inotrope score (VIS) did not significantly improve the model after accounting for the number of drugs and devices.

2. Stage D now captures additional patients with significant hypoperfusion

One important refinement concerns patients with lactate >5–10 mmol/L who are not yet receiving vasoactive drugs or temporary circulatory support.

These patients can now be assigned stage D, addressing a gap in the previous classification.

Patients already receiving one or two circulatory support treatments may also qualify for stage D if hypotension or elevated lactate persists despite treatment.

This distinction is clinically relevant because apparently acceptable blood pressure does not necessarily exclude ongoing shock or inadequate tissue perfusion.

3. Cardiac arrest is classified differently

The updated approach makes an important distinction between out-of-hospital and in-hospital cardiac arrest.

Out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) is no longer an automatic indication for stage E. Instead, it functions as a risk modifier, allowing patients to be staged according to their current hemodynamic and metabolic status.

In-hospital cardiac arrest (IHCA) was associated with particularly high mortality, frequently exceeding 50%, supporting an automatic stage E designation in clinical assessment.

This distinction may improve serial evaluation of patients who survive cardiac arrest and subsequently stabilize.

How Well Does the New Classification Stratify Mortality?

The external healthcare-system dataset demonstrated a clear, progressive increase in observed in-hospital mortality across the five stages.

2026 CSWG stage

In-hospital mortality

A – At risk

4.8%

B – Beginning shock

14.0%

C – Classic shock

21.9%

D – Deteriorating shock

34.1%

E – Extremis

59.8%

These results demonstrate that a simplified classification can distinguish clinically meaningful levels of risk.

The mortality gradient was observed in both HF-CS and MI-CS, supporting the use of a common staging framework despite their different clinical characteristics.

Compared with the 2022 system, the new criteria also led to substantial reclassification of patients previously categorized as stage D (28.4%) or stage E (approximately 56%).

Patients reclassified into less severe stages generally demonstrated lower observed mortality, suggesting more appropriate severity categorization.

An Important Finding: Stage B Is Not Benign

One of the most clinically relevant findings concerns patients with early or beginning shock.

In the updated CSWG framework, stage B can include patients with isolated hypotension or mildly elevated lactate, even before conventional features of classic shock are fully established.

In the external cohort, mortality was:

  • 13.6% in patients with isolated mild lactate elevation.

  • 16.2% in patients with isolated hypotension.

  • 21.9% in stage C patients with combined hypotension and hypoperfusion.

Furthermore, 30.1% of patients initially classified as stage B progressed to more advanced shock stages during hospitalization.

These findings emphasize the importance of recognizing early hemodynamic or metabolic deterioration rather than waiting for profound hypotension and established multiorgan dysfunction.

Lactate should nevertheless be interpreted in clinical context, as elevated lactate alone is not a definitive measure of cardiogenic hypoperfusion.

Shock Is Dynamic: Serial Assessment Matters

Perhaps the most important clinical message is that cardiogenic shock severity is not static.

In the external cohort:

  • 60.1% of patients initially at stage C progressed to more severe stages.

  • 30.1% of stage B patients progressed.

  • Patients who deteriorated to stage E during hospitalization experienced mortality comparable to those already presenting in stage E.

Within the CSWG registry, most changes in assigned stage occurred within the first six hours after diagnosis.

These observations reinforce the value of repeated reassessment of blood pressure, lactate, and circulatory support requirements, particularly during the early phase of shock management.

A patient's trajectory may be as clinically important as their stage at presentation.

What Does This Mean for Everyday Clinical Practice?

The revised CSWG classification offers several practical implications.

First, it simplifies communication. A common, objective staging language may improve consistency across emergency departments, cardiac intensive care units, catheterization laboratories, and multidisciplinary shock teams.

Second, it encourages early recognition. Patients with isolated hypotension or mild lactate elevation may still be at substantial risk, even before they meet traditional criteria for classic cardiogenic shock.

Third, it emphasizes the response to treatment. Persistent hypotension or lactate elevation despite circulatory support indicates a more severe clinical phenotype than normalization of these parameters on similar treatment.

Fourth, it supports serial risk assessment. Repeated staging may help clinicians recognize worsening trajectories and inform discussions about further evaluation or escalation of care.

Finally, it may improve clinical research. Standardized, reproducible severity criteria can help characterize trial populations and facilitate comparisons across studies and hospitals.

Importantly, the staging system is not a treatment algorithm. A higher stage does not automatically establish which vasoactive medication, device, or intervention should be selected.

Important Limitations

Despite the impressive sample size, several limitations deserve attention.

The analysis was retrospective, and treatment choices were not standardized between participating hospitals. Missing clinical data and differences in how patients were identified may have influenced the findings.

The number of vasoactive drugs and devices may reflect local practice patterns and availability as well as the underlying severity of shock.

In addition, the study assessed associations with observed in-hospital mortality rather than demonstrating that stage-guided treatment decisions improve outcomes.

The classification should therefore complement, not replace, comprehensive clinical evaluation, including hemodynamic assessment, organ perfusion, cardiac function, and the underlying cause of shock.

Prospective studies are still needed to establish whether implementation of the updated system improves clinical decision-making and patient outcomes.

The Bottom Line

The 2026 CSWG update represents an important evolution toward more practical, data-driven cardiogenic shock staging.

By focusing on systolic blood pressure, serum lactate, and treatment intensity, the new framework reduces complexity while preserving a meaningful gradient of observed mortality across stages A-E.

Three messages stand out for clinicians:

  1. Recognize shock early. Even stage B is associated with substantial mortality and risk of progression.

  2. Assess the trajectory, not just the initial stage. Clinical deterioration during hospitalization carries major prognostic implications.

  3. Use staging as a common clinical language. The classification supports risk assessment and communication but does not replace individualized clinical judgment.

The overarching message is clear: identifying cardiogenic shock severity early, monitoring its evolution, and recognizing patients who are deteriorating remain essential components of contemporary shock care.

references.title: Ton V, Li S, Zweck E et al., Updated Staging System to Define Cardiogenic Shock Severity A Cardiogenic Shock Working Group Report, Journal of Cardiac Failure, 2026
